claims.text: A self-forming, continuous, multicomponent passivating oxide scale enables a lightweight HEA to combine low density with strength, corrosion resistance, and oxidation resistance.
The proposed protective scale arises through selective oxidation of alloying elements.
Differences in atomic size and redox potential govern selective oxidation during oxide-film evolution.
Light elements with high oxygen affinity migrate or segregate to the surface during high-temperature exposure.
A coherent and adherent oxide layer restricts further oxidation and oxygen ingress.
The protective oxide layer restricts corrosive attack.
The protective oxide layer preserves the underlying alloy microstructure during exposure.
The protective oxide layer supports sustained mechanical strength after high-temperature or corrosive exposure.
The target lightweight HEA has a homogeneous single-phase microstructure in its as-cast or as-processed state.
The structural mediator is a continuous, ultrathin, multicomponent scale enriched in protective oxides such as Al2O3, Cr2O3, or analogous mixed oxides.
A similar-density baseline HEA lacking the selected oxide-forming element or elements will not form an equally protective scale.
The engineered HEA will exhibit significantly lower oxidation weight gain than the baseline alloy.
The engineered HEA will develop a more intact passivating oxide layer than the baseline alloy.
The engineered HEA will exhibit lower corrosion current density than the baseline alloy.
The engineered HEA will retain mechanical strength better than the baseline alloy after exposure.
The baseline alloy will show more extensive oxidation, poorer surface integrity, and earlier mechanical degradation under identical conditions.
A protective oxide mechanism can remain effective for exposures lasting up to a few hundred hours at temperatures where the scale remains coherent.
At excessively high temperatures or extreme oxygen partial pressures, oxide instability or spallation can eliminate the alloy's protective advantage.
Existing HEA oxidation studies show that oxide composition and protective-scale formation can strongly influence oxidation kinetics.
